### Human review and Phase Two handoff {#rd03-handoff}

The available records now support a reproducible analysis of the **selected,
recorded clump cohort**, retaining all 692 rows. They do not resolve whether the
workbook was assembled only from surviving or otherwise eligible clumps. We
found no original enrollment roster, mortality/absence ledger, per-visit leader
IDs, or inclusion probabilities in the workbook, import/model sources, Methods,
work log, or relevant repository notes; the workbook has no cell comments or
additional sheets documenting those events. The tally of roughly 25 clumps per
species per macro plot is insufficient to reconstruct an attrition denominator.
These are missing field-history evidence, not failed numerical checks.

Human review on 6 November 2026 confirmed the recorded cohort as the intended
target and defined the indicator as a residual redwood tree left on the clump
following harvest. GS has no such trees because all trees were cut. Unequal
counts may reflect too few available clumps in some blocks; no original roster
was supplied to verify that explanation. No sampling weights,
zero-height replacements, survival claims, or unobserved leader histories have
been inferred. If new field information changes inclusion or measurements,
refresh the export and this audit before fitting.

The next agent should read this section and the [candidate plan](#rd03-model-plan),
verify export integrity with
`python publication/scripts/check-analysis.py --inputs-only --protected`, and use
`inputs/thesis/sprouts/measurements.rds` in the publication environment. Preserve
the exported factor coding and original ID crosswalk; use all rows, not the
tallest-ten subset. The historical frames and 24 prediction cells provide
reproduction references, not publication estimates. Start Phase Two with the
thesis reference fits and the limited site-blocking, species-macro covariance,
and increment temporal-mean alternatives on identical rows. Use ML for
fixed-effect comparisons, retain design clustering, and record convergence,
Hessian, variance boundaries, second-optimizer agreement, and leave-one-site-out
sensitivity. Do not add an unidentified full two-period covariance on top of
unrestricted residual variances and a clump intercept.

Before reporting publication means, resolve observed-site versus exchangeable-site
standardization and predeclare contrast families and multiplicity handling.
Keep residual-tree adjustment as an explicitly conditional sensitivity, subject
to the GS overlap limitation. Bootstrap calibration and
final displays follow model review; RT02, M02, and D02 remain queued. Human
review should precede the next phase.

Phase One establishes traceable inputs and exposes a consequential selection
limitation that complete analytical frames alone concealed. It also recovers a
sampling indicator that can inform a carefully bounded sensitivity. The main
scientific limitation remains generalization beyond the selected recorded clumps;
model fitting cannot recover the missing field history or establish survival.

## Phase Two: which models should we carry forward? {#rd03-phase-two}

We want to answer two questions: how tall were the leading sprouts after ten
years, and did their annual height change slow between the two measurement
periods? We also ask whether a redwood tree left on the same clump helps explain
the sprouts' development. We use all 692 recorded clumps. These are the clumps
approved for this analysis; they do not tell us how many other clumps survived
or how much regeneration grew across a whole stand.

This review follows **model purpose → results → decision**. A model kept
"for comparison" is a useful benchmark for checking whether another model changes
the answer. It is not another recommended main model. We use that wording
instead of saying that we "retain a sensitivity."

The main comparisons give each of the four observed sites equal weight. When
we report a mean height, we mean the ordinary average in metres, allowing for
the model's estimated variation among macro plots. The intervals in this phase
are approximate: they do not yet include all the uncertainty in that estimated
variation. The completed [Phase Three analysis](#rd03-phase-three-analysis)
below reports the later checks and bootstrap results. This rewrite reviews
the existing fits; it does not fit more models.

### Reading the model formulas and AIC scores

The same terms recur throughout, so we explain them once here:

- `ht10` is tallest-sprout height at year 10, in metres. `ht_inc` is annual
  height change within a period, in m/year. The leading stem can change between
  visits, so this need not be growth of the same individual stem.
- `treat` is GS, LD, HA, or HD. `spp` distinguishes redwood (`SESE`) from tanoak
  (`LIDE`). `period` is years 1–5 (code 5) or years 5–10 (code 10).
- `a * b` includes both terms and lets the effect of one depend on the other.
  Thus `treat * spp` lets treatments have different effects on the two species.
  `treat * spp * period` also lets the amount of slowing differ among treatments
  and species.
- `site` gives each of our four sites its own adjustment. `(1 | site)` instead
  treats these as four examples from a wider population of sites and estimates
  how much sites vary. We prefer the first approach for conclusions about these
  four sites.
- `(1 | plot)` lets macro plots sit above or below the treatment mean.
  `plot` means a treatment-unit macro plot here. `(1 | tree)` does the same for
  repeatedly measured clumps; despite its name, `tree` identifies the clump.
- `(0 + spp | plot)` gives each species its own macro-plot adjustment and
  estimates whether the two adjustments move together. `diag(0 + spp | plot)`
  keeps the separate adjustments but does not estimate that connection.
- `dispformula` controls the scatter around the fitted means, not the means
  themselves. For example, `~ spp * treat` allows a different amount of scatter
  for each species–treatment group.

The height models start with `family = gaussian("log")`: average height is
modeled through a log link, while errors are measured on the original metre
scale. This keeps the fitted mean positive, but simulated individual heights
can still be negative. Growth models start with `family = gaussian()`, so they
model changes directly in m/year and can represent either increases or decreases.

**AIC helps compare fit while charging a model for extra fitted parameters. Lower
is better, including when scores are negative.** A small difference of one or
two points gives little reason to favor one model strongly; a much larger
difference is more persuasive. AIC is a ranking among the models tested, not a
test that the winner is correct. We compare height models with height models
and growth models with growth models, using the same response records and
fitting method. We never compare a height AIC with a growth AIC. The
[R AIC documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/AIC.html)
sets out that same-data requirement.

### Fitting and prediction helpers

These folded helpers apply the same fitting checks and prediction calculations
to every model. A saved model is required for recomputation;
only `refit:true` authorizes the complete fitting sequence. The focused
`refit_temporal:true` mode fits the added species-specific temporal-macro
candidates, their optimizer checks, and site omissions while reading every other
saved fit. We retain warnings and unsuccessful numerical
fits in the register rather than quietly discarding them. Model RDS files remain
ignored; tables and diagnostic figures remain versioned.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-phase-two-setup
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show fitting and prediction helpers"
suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(glmmTMB); library(ggplot2); library(DHARMa) })
p2 <- "outputs/sprouts/phase-two"
p2_read <- function(name) read.csv(file.path(p2, "tables", paste0(name, ".csv")), check.names = FALSE)
p2_write <- function(x, name) write.csv(x, file.path(p2, "tables", paste0(name, ".csv")), row.names = FALSE)
if (recompute) {
  for (folder in c("models", "tables", "figures"))
    dir.create(file.path(p2, folder), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  wide <- readRDS(file.path(input, "measurements.rds"))
  inc <- bind_rows(mutate(wide, period = "5", ht_inc = ht_inc5),
                   mutate(wide, period = "10", ht_inc = ht_inc10)) |>
    mutate(period = factor(period, levels = c("5", "10")))
  stopifnot(nrow(wide) == 692L, nrow(inc) == 1384L, !anyNA(wide$ht10), !anyNA(inc$ht_inc))
  fits <- list(); fit_records <- list(); fit_data <- list()
}
rd_fit <- function(id, mean, dispersion, data, endpoint, stage = "candidate",
                   family = gaussian(if (endpoint == "height") "log" else "identity"),
                   second_optimizer = FALSE) {
  path <- file.path(p2, "models", paste0(id, ".rds"))
  if (isTRUE(params$refit) || (isTRUE(params$refit_temporal) && grepl("^i_(LIDE|SESE)_macro", id))) {
    message("RD03 fitting ", id)
    warnings <- character()
    control <- if (second_optimizer)
      glmmTMBControl(optimizer = optim, optArgs = list(method = "BFGS"),
                     optCtrl = list(maxit = 10000, reltol = 1e-10), rank_check = "stop") else
      glmmTMBControl(optCtrl = list(iter.max = 3000, eval.max = 5000), rank_check = "stop")
    m <- withCallingHandlers(glmmTMB(mean, dispformula = dispersion, data = data,
      family = family, REML = FALSE, na.action = na.fail, control = control),
      warning = function(w) { warnings <<- c(warnings, conditionMessage(w)); invokeRestart("muffleWarning") })
    attr(m, "rd03_warnings") <- paste(unique(warnings), collapse = "; ")
    saveRDS(m, path)
  } else {
    if (!file.exists(path)) stop("Missing saved RD03 fit: ", id, ". Explicit refit:true is required.")
    m <- readRDS(path)
  }
  stopifnot(nobs(m) == nrow(data), identical(rownames(model.frame(m)), rownames(data)))
  if ("tree" %in% names(model.frame(m)))
    stopifnot(identical(as.character(model.frame(m)$tree), as.character(data$tree)))
  ll <- logLik(m)
  fit_records[[id]] <<- data.frame(model_id = id, stage = stage, endpoint = endpoint,
    fit_status = "fit", n = nobs(m), n_clumps = n_distinct(data$tree), n_sites = n_distinct(data$site),
    mean = paste(deparse(formula(m)), collapse = " "),
    dispersion = paste(deparse(formula(m, component = "disp")), collapse = " "),
    family = family(m)$family, link = family(m)$link, parameters = attr(ll, "df"),
    log_likelihood = as.numeric(ll), AIC = AIC(m), convergence = m$fit$convergence,
    pd_hessian = isTRUE(m$sdr$pdHess), max_gradient = max(abs(m$sdr$gradient.fixed)),
    warnings = attr(m, "rd03_warnings"))
  fits[[id]] <<- m
  fit_data[[id]] <<- data
  m
}
rd_usable <- function(m) m$fit$convergence == 0 && isTRUE(m$sdr$pdHess)
rd_variance <- function(m, id) {
  bind_rows(purrr::map(names(VarCorr(m)$cond), function(group) {
    v <- VarCorr(m)$cond[[group]]
    ix <- which(lower.tri(v, diag = TRUE), arr.ind = TRUE)
    data.frame(model_id = id, group = group, term1 = rownames(v)[ix[, 1]],
      term2 = colnames(v)[ix[, 2]], covariance = v[ix],
      correlation = attr(v, "correlation")[ix],
      boundary_sd_below_1e_4 = sqrt(diag(v))[ix[, 1]] < 1e-4 | sqrt(diag(v))[ix[, 2]] < 1e-4)
  }))
}
rd_means <- function(m, data, endpoint, id) {
  stopifnot(rd_usable(m))
  grid <- expand.grid(site = levels(droplevels(data$site)), treat = levels(droplevels(data$treat)),
    spp = levels(droplevels(data$spp)),
    period = if (endpoint == "increment") levels(data$period) else "year10",
    KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  for (v in c("site", "treat", "spp")) grid[[v]] <- factor(grid[[v]], levels = levels(data[[v]]))
  if (endpoint == "increment") grid$period <- factor(grid$period, levels = levels(data$period))
  grid$plot <- data$plot[1]; grid$tree <- data$tree[1]
  ff <- delete.response(terms(lme4::nobars(formula(m))))
  X <- model.matrix(ff, grid)
  beta <- fixef(m)$cond
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(X), names(beta)))
  eta <- drop(X %*% beta)
  stopifnot(max(abs(predict(m, newdata = grid, type = "link", re.form = NA) - eta)) < 1e-8)
  multiplier <- rep(1, nrow(grid))
  vc <- VarCorr(m)$cond
  random_site <- "site" %in% names(vc)
  if (family(m)$link == "log") {
    for (i in seq_len(nrow(grid))) {
      v <- sum(purrr::map_dbl(names(vc), function(group) {
        z <- vc[[group]]
        if (nrow(z) == 1L) z[1, 1] else z[paste0("spp", grid$spp[i]), paste0("spp", grid$spp[i])]
      }))
      multiplier[i] <- exp(v / 2)
    }
  }
  mu <- family(m)$linkinv(eta) * multiplier
  J <- X * as.numeric(family(m)$mu.eta(eta) * multiplier)
  cells <- unique(grid[c("spp", "treat", "period")])
  W <- do.call(rbind, purrr::map(seq_len(nrow(cells)), function(j) {
    z <- grid$spp == cells$spp[j] & grid$treat == cells$treat[j] & grid$period == cells$period[j]
    as.numeric(z) / sum(z)
  }))
  G <- W %*% J
  covariance <- G %*% as.matrix(vcov(m)$cond) %*% t(G)
  ans <- data.frame(model_id = id, cells, estimate = drop(W %*% mu),
    se = sqrt(diag(covariance)), target = if (random_site) "exchangeable sites; random effects integrated" else
      "four observed sites equally weighted; macro effects integrated",
    uncertainty = "provisional Wald; random variances held fixed")
  ans$lcl <- ans$estimate - qnorm(.975) * ans$se
  ans$ucl <- ans$estimate + qnorm(.975) * ans$se
  list(table = ans, covariance = covariance, gradient = G,
       coefficient_covariance = as.matrix(vcov(m)$cond))
}
rd_contrasts <- function(z, endpoint) {
  a <- z$table; rows <- list()
  add <- function(w, label, spp) {
    est <- sum(w * a$estimate)
    # Form the contrast gradient first: subtracting nearly equal cell
    # covariances loses precision for changes constrained to be identical.
    g <- drop(t(w) %*% z$gradient)
    se <- sqrt(drop(t(g) %*% z$coefficient_covariance %*% g))
    rows[[length(rows) + 1L]] <<- data.frame(model_id = a$model_id[1], spp = spp,
      contrast = label, estimate = est, se = se, lcl = est - qnorm(.975) * se,
      ucl = est + qnorm(.975) * se, uncertainty = a$uncertainty[1])
  }
  for (sp in unique(as.character(a$spp))) {
    if (endpoint == "height") {
      for (tr in c("GS", "HA")) add(as.numeric(a$spp == sp & a$treat == tr) -
        as.numeric(a$spp == sp & a$treat == "HD"), paste0(tr, " minus HD height"), sp)
    } else {
      changes <- purrr::map(levels(wide$treat), function(tr)
        as.numeric(a$spp == sp & a$treat == tr & a$period == "10") -
        as.numeric(a$spp == sp & a$treat == tr & a$period == "5"))
      names(changes) <- levels(wide$treat)
      for (tr in names(changes)) add(changes[[tr]], paste0(tr, " later minus earlier"), sp)
      for (tr in c("GS", "HA")) add(changes[[tr]] - changes$HD,
        paste0(tr, " minus HD period change"), sp)
    }
  }
  bind_rows(rows)
}
```

### First models: height and growth with both species together

We begin with models that include both species in one fit. The names in code
font are the exact model IDs used in the results tables and saved files.

**Height model `h_reference` reproduces the thesis starting model.** It
lets treatment effects differ between species, allows linked species responses
within a macro plot, and estimates a separate amount of variation among sites.
All three height models below use `gaussian("log")` and the same
`dispformula = ~ spp * treat`.

```r
# h_reference
ht10 ~ treat * spp + (0 + spp | plot) + (1 | site)
```

**`h_fixed` replaces `(1 | site)` with `site`.** Instead of trying to
describe a wider population of sites from only four examples, we give the four
observed sites their own adjustments. The treatment question is otherwise the same.

```r
# h_fixed — replace the site term in h_reference
ht10 ~ treat * spp + (0 + spp | plot) + site
```

**`h_diagonal` removes the estimated connection between species' macro-plot
adjustments.** Redwood and tanoak can still vary by different amounts among
macro plots. This asks whether estimating that extra connection helps enough
to justify keeping it.

```r
# h_diagonal — replace the macro-plot term in h_fixed
ht10 ~ treat * spp + diag(0 + spp | plot) + site
```

**Growth model `i_reference` reproduces the thesis growth model.** Its
`period * spp` term lets each species grow more slowly in the later period,
but forces that amount of slowing to be the same under every treatment within
the species. It includes repeated-clump and macro-plot adjustments, but no site
term. All four growth models below use `gaussian()` and
`dispformula = ~ spp * period * treat`.

```r
# i_reference
ht_inc ~ treat * spp + period * spp + (1 | tree) + (0 + spp | plot)
```

**`i_fixed` adds `site`; `i_diagonal` then simplifies the species link
within macro plots, just as `h_diagonal` did.** These changes account for the four study
sites and check whether the cross-species connection is needed. Neither change
allows slowing to differ among treatments yet.

```r
# i_fixed — add site to i_reference
ht_inc ~ treat * spp + period * spp + site + (1 | tree) + (0 + spp | plot)

# i_diagonal — simplify the macro-plot term in i_fixed
ht_inc ~ treat * spp + period * spp + site + (1 | tree) + diag(0 + spp | plot)
```

**`i_full` replaces the mean terms with `treat * spp * period`.** Now GS,
LD, HA, and HD can have different amounts of slowing in each species. This is
the first of these joint models that can directly answer whether treatments
differ in how growth changed between periods.

```r
# i_full — allow treatment-specific change between periods
ht_inc ~ treat * spp * period + site + (1 | tree) + diag(0 + spp | plot)
```

The table compares these models and the additional checks described after it.
`convergence = 0` and `pd_hessian = TRUE` mean that the fitting checks did not
identify a numerical failure. They are prerequisites for using a fit, not
evidence that its assumptions are right. The folded fitting code preserves all
the tested specifications for review.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-joint-candidates
if (recompute) {
  rd_fit("h_reference", ht10 ~ treat * spp + (0 + spp | plot) + (1 | site), ~spp * treat, wide, "height")
  rd_fit("h_fixed", ht10 ~ treat * spp + site + (0 + spp | plot), ~spp * treat, wide, "height")
  rd_fit("h_diagonal", ht10 ~ treat * spp + site + diag(0 + spp | plot), ~spp * treat, wide, "height")
  rd_fit("h_disp_add", ht10 ~ treat * spp + site + diag(0 + spp | plot), ~spp + treat, wide, "height")
  rd_fit("h_identity", ht10 ~ treat * spp + site + diag(0 + spp | plot), ~spp * treat, wide, "height", family = gaussian())
  rd_fit("h_gamma", ht10 ~ treat * spp + site + diag(0 + spp | plot), ~spp * treat, wide, "height", family = Gamma(link = "log"))
  rd_fit("i_reference", ht_inc ~ treat * spp + period * spp + (1 | tree) + (0 + spp | plot), ~spp * period * treat, inc, "increment")
  rd_fit("i_random", ht_inc ~ treat * spp + period * spp + (1 | site) + (1 | tree) + (0 + spp | plot), ~spp * period * treat, inc, "increment")
  rd_fit("i_fixed", ht_inc ~ treat * spp + period * spp + site + (1 | tree) + (0 + spp | plot), ~spp * period * treat, inc, "increment")
  rd_fit("i_diagonal", ht_inc ~ treat * spp + period * spp + site + (1 | tree) + diag(0 + spp | plot), ~spp * period * treat, inc, "increment")
  rd_fit("i_full", ht_inc ~ treat * spp * period + site + (1 | tree) + diag(0 + spp | plot), ~spp * period * treat, inc, "increment")
  rd_fit("i_disp_period", ht_inc ~ treat * spp * period + site + (1 | tree) + diag(0 + spp | plot), ~spp * period, inc, "increment")
  rd_fit("i_disp_add", ht_inc ~ treat * spp * period + site + (1 | tree) + diag(0 + spp | plot), ~spp * period + treat, inc, "increment")
  joint_ids <- names(fits)
  p2_write(bind_rows(fit_records), "joint-comparison")
  reference_check <- bind_rows(purrr::map(c("h_reference", "i_reference"), function(id) {
    endpoint <- if (startsWith(id, "h")) "height" else "increment"
    nd <- if (endpoint == "height") wide else inc
    historical <- read.csv(file.path(input, "historical-predictions.csv")) |>
      filter(model_id == if (endpoint == "height") "ht10_sel" else "minc_sel")
    grid <- nd[rep(1L, nrow(historical)), ]
    grid$treat <- factor(historical$treat, levels = levels(nd$treat))
    grid$spp <- factor(historical$spp, levels = levels(nd$spp))
    if (endpoint == "increment") grid$period <- factor(historical$period, levels = levels(nd$period))
    delta <- max(abs(predict(fits[[id]], grid, re.form = NA, type = "response") - historical$estimate))
    # Cross-version numerical reproduction tolerance; no analytical inputs change.
    stopifnot(delta < 1e-4)
    data.frame(model_id = id, cells = nrow(historical), max_absolute_prediction_error = delta,
      tolerance = 1e-4, passed = delta < 1e-4)
  }))
  p2_write(reference_check, "reference-reproduction")
}
knitr::kable(p2_read("joint-comparison") |>
  transmute(Model = model_id, Response = endpoint, Rows = n, Parameters = parameters,
    AIC, `Fitting checks OK` = convergence == 0 & pd_hessian), digits = 2)
```

The reproduction check asks whether `h_reference` and `i_reference`
recover the thesis predictions. If they did not, we would need to resolve that
problem before interpreting differences caused by our model changes.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-reference-reproduction-review
knitr::kable(p2_read("reference-reproduction"), digits = 7)
```

**Results.** `h_reference` and `i_reference` reproduce all 24 thesis prediction cells to within the
declared tolerance. The largest height difference is less than 0.000004 m, so
reproducing the starting analysis is not a concern.

For height, `h_reference` (AIC 2718.08) leads this first set. `h_fixed` (AIC 2721.13) and `h_diagonal` (AIC 2721.60) are close to each other: estimating the
species connection in `h_fixed` improves AIC by only 0.47. `h_reference` estimates almost no
between-site variation. That does not make the four-site design unimportant;
it means these records provide little information for estimating a wider
population of sites. **We carry `h_fixed` and `h_diagonal` into the comparison with separate
species models below.** `h_reference` remains the thesis benchmark.

For growth, `i_reference` (AIC -655.30) leads the joint fits. `i_diagonal`
(AIC -651.31) and `i_full` (AIC -644.89) fit less well after accounting
for their extra parameters. The 6.42-point increase from `i_diagonal` to `i_full` gives little
support, within this model structure, for separate amounts of slowing in each
treatment. **We keep `i_full` as a comparison because it asks our full treatment/time
question, then check whether separate species models describe the data better.**
`i_diagonal` cannot establish equal slowing: it assumes it in the formula.

The remaining first-round models are not leading candidates. `h_identity`
changes the height link; `h_gamma` changes the height distribution;
`h_disp_add` shares more of the scatter estimates across groups. Their AICs
are 5.64, 24.86, and 11.10 points worse than `h_diagonal`, respectively. `i_random` adds
a site-variation estimate to `i_reference` but estimates almost none and improves nothing.
`i_disp_period` and `i_disp_add` share more growth-scatter estimates across groups
and both perform worse than `i_full`. We do not carry these alternatives forward as
main-model candidates. `h_gamma` remains useful in the diagnostic review because
it avoids impossible negative heights, letting us see the cost of that choice.

### Do separate redwood and tanoak models work better?

The joint models above make some things common to both species. For example,
`i_full` gives redwood and tanoak the same amount of persistent variation
among clumps and the same site adjustment. We now ask whether that is too
restrictive. Each formula below is fitted once to redwood (`SESE`) and once
to tanoak (`LIDE`), using the same records as before.

**Height models `h_SESE` and `h_LIDE` separate the two species.** Each now
has its own treatment effects, site adjustments, and amount of macro-plot and
remaining variation. There is no `spp` term because only one species is in each fit.

```r
# h_SESE for redwood; h_LIDE for tanoak
ht10 ~ treat + site + (1 | plot)
# family = gaussian("log"); dispformula = ~ treat
```

**Growth models `i_SESE` and `i_LIDE` also separate the species.** Compared
with `i_full`, this lets their clumps vary by different amounts and gives each species
its own site adjustments. Treatment-specific slowing remains in `treat * period`.

```r
# i_SESE for redwood; i_LIDE for tanoak
ht_inc ~ treat * period + site + (1 | plot) + (1 | tree)
# family = gaussian(); dispformula = ~ treat * period
```

**`i_SESE_us` and `i_LIDE_us` check a different way to connect the two
measurements from a clump.** Instead of a shared clump adjustment that always
moves the two periods in the same direction, `us(0 + period | tree)` estimates
the two periods' variation and connection directly. They could move in opposite
directions. We remove the separate estimated error term with `dispformula = ~0`
to avoid estimating the same variation twice.

```r
# i_SESE_us and i_LIDE_us
ht_inc ~ treat * period + site + (1 | plot) + us(0 + period | tree)
# family = gaussian(); dispformula = ~0
```

For a fair comparison with `i_SESE_us` and `i_LIDE_us`, the existing `i_SESE_period` and `i_LIDE_period`
fits use the formula from `i_SESE` and `i_LIDE` but `dispformula = ~ period`.
Like `i_SESE_us` and `i_LIDE_us`, they share the two
periods' within-clump variation estimates across treatments. This comparison
asks whether allowing an opposite-direction connection helps, rather than
changing that question and the treatment scatter estimates together.

**`i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro` change the macro-plot term used in
`i_SESE` and `i_LIDE`.** A
single `(1 | plot)` contribution is the same in both periods, so it cancels
when we subtract one period from the other. `(0 + period | plot)` lets a macro
plot contribute differently in each period. For example, one treatment unit
may slow more than another even after allowing for their clump differences.
That variation belongs in the uncertainty about treatment-level slowing.

```r
# i_SESE_macro and i_LIDE_macro
ht_inc ~ treat * period + site + (0 + period | plot) + (1 | tree)
# family = gaussian(); dispformula = ~ treat * period
```

The ten-row table shows each species' fit separately. Use it to compare a
model change within redwood or within tanoak. The combined table immediately
after it is the appropriate comparison with the joint models.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-species-covariance
if (recompute) {
  for (sp in levels(wide$spp)) {
    h <- droplevels(filter(wide, spp == sp)); ii <- droplevels(filter(inc, spp == sp))
    rd_fit(paste0("h_", sp), ht10 ~ treat + site + (1 | plot), ~treat, h, "height")
    rd_fit(paste0("i_", sp), ht_inc ~ treat * period + site + (1 | plot) + (1 | tree), ~treat * period, ii, "increment")
    rd_fit(paste0("i_", sp, "_period"), ht_inc ~ treat * period + site + (1 | plot) + (1 | tree), ~period, ii, "increment")
    rd_fit(paste0("i_", sp, "_us"), ht_inc ~ treat * period + site + (1 | plot) + us(0 + period | tree), ~0, ii, "increment")
    rd_fit(paste0("i_", sp, "_macro"), ht_inc ~ treat * period + site + (0 + period | plot) + (1 | tree), ~treat * period, ii, "increment")
  }
  p2_write(bind_rows(fit_records) |> filter(!model_id %in% joint_ids), "species-comparison")
  p2_write(bind_rows(purrr::map(names(fits), function(id) rd_variance(fits[[id]], id))), "variance-components")
}
knitr::kable(p2_read("species-comparison") |>
  transmute(Model = model_id, Response = endpoint, Rows = n, Parameters = parameters,
    AIC, `Fitting checks OK` = convergence == 0 & pd_hessian), digits = 2)
```

To compare a pair of separate fits with a joint fit, we add their log-likelihoods
and parameter counts. AIC is `-2 * log_likelihood + 2 * parameters`, so the pair's
combined AIC is also the sum of its two AIC values. We do **not** compare the
redwood-only AIC with a joint model fitted to both species. Each pair below
covers the same full height or growth records as its joint competitors and
uses the same likelihood method. Treating the pair as one model assumes no
additional shared random effect linking the two species.

The following calculation uses only the saved fit tables. It does not fit or
update any model. `AIC above leader` shows the distance from the lowest score
within the height or growth comparison.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-combined-aic-review
joint <- p2_read("joint-comparison")
separate <- p2_read("species-comparison")
pair_ids <- list(
  h_separate = c("h_SESE", "h_LIDE"),
  i_separate = c("i_SESE", "i_LIDE"),
  i_period_separate = c("i_SESE_period", "i_LIDE_period"),
  i_us_separate = c("i_SESE_us", "i_LIDE_us"),
  i_macro_separate = c("i_SESE_macro", "i_LIDE_macro"))
pair_scores <- bind_rows(purrr::map(names(pair_ids), function(id) {
  x <- separate[match(pair_ids[[id]], separate$model_id), ]
  stopifnot(nrow(x) == 2L, !anyNA(x$model_id), all(x$convergence == 0),
    all(x$pd_hessian), length(unique(x$family)) == 1L, length(unique(x$link)) == 1L)
  score <- -2 * sum(x$log_likelihood) + 2 * sum(x$parameters)
  stopifnot(abs(score - sum(x$AIC)) < 1e-8)
  data.frame(model_id = id, endpoint = x$endpoint[1], models = paste(x$model_id, collapse = " + "),
    n = sum(x$n), parameters = sum(x$parameters),
    log_likelihood = sum(x$log_likelihood), AIC = score)
}))
joint_scores <- joint |> filter(model_id %in% c("h_reference", "h_fixed", "h_diagonal",
  "i_reference", "i_fixed", "i_diagonal", "i_full", "i_disp_period")) |>
  transmute(model_id, endpoint, models = model_id, n, parameters, log_likelihood, AIC)
combined_aic <- bind_rows(joint_scores, pair_scores) |>
  group_by(endpoint) |> mutate(delta_aic = AIC - min(AIC)) |> ungroup() |>
  arrange(endpoint, AIC)
stopifnot(all(combined_aic$n[combined_aic$endpoint == "height"] == 692L),
  all(combined_aic$n[combined_aic$endpoint == "increment"] == 1384L))
p2_write(combined_aic, "combined-aic-comparison")
knitr::kable(combined_aic |> select(endpoint, models, parameters, AIC, delta_aic), digits = 2,
  col.names = c("Response", "Model or pair", "Parameters", "AIC", "AIC above leader"))
```

**Results and decision for height.** The pair `h_SESE` and `h_LIDE` has combined AIC
2719.75. It is only 1.38 points better than `h_fixed` and 1.85 better than
`h_diagonal`, while `h_reference` remains slightly lower at 2718.08.
This is a close group, not an overwhelming AIC win for `h_SESE` and `h_LIDE`. **We recommend `h_SESE` and `h_LIDE`
for the next review because they let each species have its own site response
and are straightforward to explain.** `h_fixed` and `h_diagonal` remain useful comparisons to
check that this choice does not drive the reported height differences.

**Results and decision for growth.** The pair `i_SESE` and `i_LIDE` has combined AIC
-740.88, about 96 points better than `i_full` (AIC -644.89). Giving the species
their own variation estimates makes a large improvement. The pair `i_SESE_macro`
and `i_LIDE_macro` improves the combined score by another 25.93 points, to -766.81.
**`i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro` form the clear leading pair among these existing growth models
and are the models we recommend carrying forward.** `i_full`, `i_SESE`, and `i_LIDE` remain comparisons for understanding
how the added terms change uncertainty, not equally strong main candidates.

The pair `i_SESE_us` and `i_LIDE_us`, and the matching pair `i_SESE_period` and
`i_LIDE_period`, both score -730.81. Allowing the two clump measurements to move in opposite
directions brings no improvement here. Both pairs also score worse than the
`i_SESE`/`i_LIDE` pair and the `i_SESE_macro`/`i_LIDE_macro` pair. We do not carry
`i_SESE_us`, `i_LIDE_us`, or the `_period` pair forward as leading models.

### What the variation estimates tell us about those choices

We produced the variance table to understand *why* the models differ, rather
than choose a model from its AIC alone. The important findings are these:

- **`i_full` forces the same amount of clump-to-clump growth variation
  in both species. `i_SESE` and `i_LIDE` show much more in redwood.**
  On the growth-rate scale, `i_full`'s shared spread is about 0.116 m/year, while `i_SESE` and `i_LIDE`
  estimate about 0.215 for redwood and 0.089 for tanoak. These are standard
  deviations (the square roots of the variances in the table): larger values
  mean greater persistent differences among clumps after accounting for
  treatment and site. Letting those amounts differ helps explain the large
  combined AIC improvement from `i_SESE` and `i_LIDE`.
- **`i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro` allow macro plots to slow by
  different amounts.** Their estimated between-macro variation in the change
  between periods has an SD of about 0.063 m/year for redwood and 0.042 for
  tanoak. The single macro adjustment in `i_SESE` and `i_LIDE` forces this contribution to the period
  difference to be zero. That is why we prefer `i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro` when reporting how much
  growth slowed and how uncertain that amount is.
- **`i_SESE_us` and `i_LIDE_us` estimate positive connections between a
  clump's two periods**, about 0.615 for redwood and 0.405 for tanoak. The
  connection is not negative, and their fits are essentially identical to
  `i_SESE_period` and `i_LIDE_period`. We have no reason here to prefer the more
  flexible way `i_SESE_us` and `i_LIDE_us` connect the two clump measurements.
- **`h_fixed` and `h_diagonal` differ mainly in a species connection
  that buys little fit improvement.** `h_reference` estimates almost zero
  variation among sites. Neither finding is a reason to erase the four-site
  experimental design; `h_SESE` and `h_LIDE` keep separate adjustments for those observed sites.

These findings support `h_SESE`, `h_LIDE`, `i_SESE_macro`, and `i_LIDE_macro` as
the next models to review, with the strongest improvement belonging to the
growth-model pair. A remaining concern is whether the extra macro-period terms
in `i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro` can be fitted reliably with only four sites; we check
that below. The full table is folded because its many repeated entries obscure
these few useful comparisons.

<details>
<summary>Show all variance and correlation estimates</summary>

```{r}
#| label: rd03-variance-components-review
knitr::kable(p2_read("variance-components"), digits = 4)
```

</details>

The complete table adds detail but no further main-model recommendation. In
particular, a small variance estimate is not proof that a grouping level never
matters, and these two visits cannot separate measurement error from every
other source of variation within a clump.

### A residual tree on the clump

Could a redwood tree left on a clump help or hinder the basal sprouts? We can
ask that question in LD, HA, and HD, where clumps with and without residual trees
exist. We cannot make that comparison in GS because all its trees were cut.
The indicator is not defined for tanoak.

For height, `rh_base` uses the `h_SESE` formula on just these three treatments.
`rh_residual` adds `residual_rw`, estimating one common association across them.
For growth, `ri_base` uses the `i_SESE` formula on the same restricted cohort;
`ri_residual` adds `residual_rw * period`, allowing the association to differ
between the two periods. The other terms and scatter formulas stay the same.

```r
# rh_residual: add residual-tree status to rh_base
ht10 ~ treat + site + residual_rw + (1 | plot)

# ri_residual: add residual-tree status and its period difference to ri_base
ht_inc ~ treat * period + site + residual_rw * period + (1 | plot) + (1 | tree)
```

The fit table asks whether these additions explain enough variation to be
worth the extra terms. Each comparison uses the same 243 redwood clumps.
It describes an association: clumps with residual trees might also differ in
local conditions or how they were selected, so it cannot establish cause.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-residual-tree
if (recompute) {
  rh <- droplevels(filter(wide, spp == "SESE", treat != "GS"))
  ri <- droplevels(filter(inc, spp == "SESE", treat != "GS"))
  stopifnot(nrow(rh) == 243L, all(rh$residual_rw %in% c(0, 1)))
  rd_fit("rh_base", ht10 ~ treat + site + (1 | plot), ~treat, rh, "height", stage = "residual_tree")
  rd_fit("rh_residual", ht10 ~ treat + site + residual_rw + (1 | plot), ~treat, rh, "height", stage = "residual_tree")
  rd_fit("ri_base", ht_inc ~ treat * period + site + (1 | plot) + (1 | tree), ~treat * period, ri, "increment", stage = "residual_tree")
  rd_fit("ri_residual", ht_inc ~ treat * period + site + residual_rw * period + (1 | plot) + (1 | tree), ~treat * period, ri, "increment", stage = "residual_tree")
  p2_write(rh |> group_by(site, treat, residual_rw) |>
    summarise(n_clumps = n(), height10 = mean(ht10), increment_1_5 = mean(ht_inc5),
      increment_5_10 = mean(ht_inc10), .groups = "drop"), "residual-tree-observed")
  assoc <- list()
  for (id in c("rh_residual", "ri_residual")) {
    m <- fits[[id]]; beta <- fixef(m)$cond; V <- as.matrix(vcov(m)$cond)
    for (period in if (id == "rh_residual") "year10" else c("5", "10")) {
      w <- setNames(rep(0, length(beta)), names(beta)); w["residual_rw"] <- 1
      if (period == "10") w[grep("residual_rw:period10|period10:residual_rw", names(beta))] <- 1
      est <- sum(w * beta); se <- sqrt(drop(t(w) %*% V %*% w))
      logged <- id == "rh_residual"
      f <- if (logged) exp else identity
      assoc[[length(assoc) + 1L]] <- data.frame(model_id = id, period = period,
        effect = if (logged) "residual-present / absent height ratio" else "residual-present minus absent m yr-1",
        estimate = f(est), lcl = f(est - qnorm(.975) * se), ucl = f(est + qnorm(.975) * se),
        uncertainty = "exploratory Wald; selected retained-treatment clumps")
    }
  }
  p2_write(bind_rows(assoc), "residual-tree-associations")
  p2_write(bind_rows(fit_records) |> filter(stage == "residual_tree"), "residual-tree-comparison")
}
knitr::kable(p2_read("residual-tree-comparison") |>
  select(model_id, n, parameters, AIC, convergence, pd_hessian), digits = 3)
```

The association table puts the residual-tree result in biological units. A
height ratio of 1 means no estimated height difference; an increment difference
of 0 means no estimated growth-rate difference. The intervals show whether both
augmentation and suppression remain plausible.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-residual-tree-associations-review
knitr::kable(p2_read("residual-tree-associations"), digits = 4)
```

**Results and decision.** Adding the indicator raises AIC by 1.10 for
`rh_residual` and 3.36 for `ri_residual`, so neither improves the fit enough to
justify the added terms. `rh_residual` estimates about 5% greater height with a
residual tree, but its interval runs from about 5% shorter to 16% taller.
`ri_residual` estimates small growth-rate differences of +0.031 and +0.016 m/year,
with intervals allowing either a reduction or an increase.

**Leave `residual_rw` out of the main treatment models.** Keep these results as
a secondary comparison documenting what we tried; they do not show that a
residual tree has no effect. The cohort has 106 clumps without a residual tree
and 137 with one. The folded observed table records their distribution among
sites and treatments, rather than adding a new adjusted effect estimate.

<summary>Show observed clump counts and means by residual-tree status</summary>

```{r}

knitr::kable(p2_read("residual-tree-observed"), digits = 3)
```

</details>

### What do the recommended height and growth models predict?

A good AIC score does not tell us the size of a treatment difference. We now
use `h_SESE`, `h_LIDE`, `i_SESE_macro`, and `i_LIDE_macro` to put the
answers in metres and m/year. These are the recommended models, not a generic
set of predictions from unnamed "preferred structures."

We average predictions across the four sites equally. For the log-link height
models, we also allow for the estimated variation among macro plots when
returning to an ordinary mean in metres. The folded prediction code checks
its calculations against R's direct predictions. The intervals below are
approximate 95% intervals and are not adjusted for making several comparisons;
the later Phase Three results provide the bootstrap follow-up.

The first table shows how tall clumps are predicted to be under each treatment
in `h_SESE` and `h_LIDE`. The next table shows the annual rates from
`i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro` separately for the two periods.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-candidate-estimates
if (recompute) {
  prediction_ids <- c(joint_ids, "h_LIDE", "h_SESE", "i_LIDE", "i_SESE",
    "i_LIDE_period", "i_SESE_period", "i_LIDE_us", "i_SESE_us", "i_LIDE_macro", "i_SESE_macro")
  means <- contrasts <- list()
  for (id in prediction_ids) {
    m <- fits[[id]]
    if (!rd_usable(m)) next
    endpoint <- if (startsWith(id, "h")) "height" else "increment"
    dat <- if (endpoint == "height") wide else inc
    sp <- sub("^[hi]_(LIDE|SESE).*", "\\1", id)
    if (sp %in% levels(wide$spp)) dat <- droplevels(filter(dat, spp == sp))
    z <- rd_means(m, dat, endpoint, id)
    means[[id]] <- z$table; contrasts[[id]] <- rd_contrasts(z, endpoint)
    stopifnot(all(is.finite(contrasts[[id]]$estimate)), all(is.finite(contrasts[[id]]$se)))
    if (id %in% c("i_reference", "i_random", "i_fixed", "i_diagonal")) {
      zero <- filter(contrasts[[id]], grepl("minus HD period change", contrast))
      # These differences are analytically zero under the reduced mean;
      # this also checks stable SE calculation after covariance cancellation.
      stopifnot(all(abs(zero$estimate) < 1e-10), all(zero$se < 1e-8))
    }
  }
  p2_write(bind_rows(means), "candidate-means")
  p2_write(bind_rows(contrasts), "candidate-contrasts")
}
knitr::kable(p2_read("candidate-means") |> filter(model_id %in% c("h_SESE", "h_LIDE")) |>
  transmute(Model = model_id, Species = ifelse(spp == "SESE", "Redwood", "Tanoak"),
    Treatment = treat, `Height (m)` = estimate, `Lower 95% limit` = lcl, `Upper 95% limit` = ucl), digits = 3)
```

`h_SESE` estimates redwood heights of about 10.60, 8.05, 6.91, and 5.95 m under GS,
LD, HA, and HD. Redwood is tallest under GS and shortest under HD in this model.
To see how growth led toward those sizes, we keep the early and late rates from
`i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro`
separate rather than averaging away a possible change over time.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-leading-growth-rates-review
knitr::kable(p2_read("candidate-means") |>
  filter(model_id %in% c("i_SESE_macro", "i_LIDE_macro")) |>
  transmute(Model = model_id, Species = ifelse(spp == "SESE", "Redwood", "Tanoak"),
    Treatment = treat, Period = ifelse(period == "5", "Years 1–5", "Years 5–10"),
    `Annual height change (m/year)` = estimate, `Lower 95% limit` = lcl, `Upper 95% limit` = ucl), digits = 3)
```

`i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro` estimate a lower later growth rate in every treatment for both species.
That observation motivates two different comparisons: did growth slow within
each treatment, and did it slow *more* in one treatment than another? Those are
different questions. For example, evidence of slowing in GS alone does not
establish more slowing in GS than HD.

The next table directly subtracts HD height from GS or HA height in `h_SESE` and `h_LIDE`, with
`h_diagonal` included as a check on whether using separate species models
changes the answer. These direct differences are sometimes called **contrasts**;
we spell out what is subtracted in each row. They are more informative for
the treatment comparison than judging overlap between two mean-height intervals.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-joint-contrasts-review
knitr::kable(p2_read("candidate-contrasts") |> filter(model_id %in% c("h_SESE", "h_LIDE", "h_diagonal")) |>
  transmute(Model = model_id, Species = ifelse(spp == "SESE", "Redwood", "Tanoak"),
    Comparison = contrast, `Difference (m)` = estimate, `Lower 95% limit` = lcl, `Upper 95% limit` = ucl), digits = 3)
```

For redwood, `h_SESE` estimates GS minus HD at 4.65 m and HA minus HD at 0.96 m.
`h_diagonal` gives almost the same differences, 4.64 and 0.99 m. **The main height pattern
is not being created by the choice between these joint and separate models.**
The HA–HD interval includes both an advantage and a disadvantage, so a clear
benefit of aggregated over dispersed retention is not established.

The comparison table for `i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro` answers both growth
questions. A row such as "GS later
minus earlier" subtracts its years 1–5 annual rate from its years 5–10 rate;
a negative value means slowing. "GS minus HD period change" then subtracts
HD's slowing value from GS's. A negative value in that row means more slowing
in GS, not simply slower growth in GS.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-temporal-macro-contrasts-review
knitr::kable(p2_read("candidate-contrasts") |> filter(model_id %in% c("i_LIDE_macro", "i_SESE_macro")) |>
  transmute(Model = model_id, Species = ifelse(spp == "SESE", "Redwood", "Tanoak"),
    Comparison = contrast, `Difference (m/year)` = estimate, `Lower 95% limit` = lcl, `Upper 95% limit` = ucl), digits = 3)
```

`i_SESE_macro` estimates redwood slowing of about 0.159, 0.163, 0.064, and
0.120 m/year under GS, LD, HA, and HD. But the direct differences in slowing
between GS and HD (-0.039 m/year), and between HA and HD (+0.056 m/year), both
have intervals spanning zero. In `i_LIDE_macro`, even the four within-treatment
change intervals span zero. **Carry forward the height result more confidently
than a claim that treatments caused different amounts of slowing.** These
intervals do not establish equal slowing either; we have not tested a defined
margin of practical equivalence. Separate species fits also do not provide
the shared uncertainty needed for a formal redwood-versus-tanoak difference test.

### Do the fitting methods agree, and does one site drive the answer?

Before using `h_SESE`, `h_LIDE`, `i_SESE_macro`, and `i_LIDE_macro`, we need to know that their results are not numerical
accidents. The existing checks first fitted eleven models with two different
algorithms, `nlminb` and BFGS. They include `h_diagonal`, `i_SESE_macro`, and `i_LIDE_macro`;
the algorithm checks for `h_SESE` and `h_LIDE` are reported in Phase Three. If the algorithms reached
noticeably different answers, we would investigate before interpreting the fit.
All eleven Phase Two checks agree:
their largest prediction difference is less than 0.000075 in the response units.
There is no new warning here that changes the model recommendation. The detailed
table and calculation code are folded because the useful finding is that
agreement, not the many nearly zero entries.

<details>
<summary>Show the two-algorithm checks and site-omission calculation code</summary>

```{r}
#| label: rd03-optimizer-influence
if (recompute) {
  optimizer_ids <- c("h_diagonal", "h_identity", "h_gamma", "i_full", "i_disp_add",
    "i_LIDE_us", "i_SESE_us", "i_LIDE_macro", "i_SESE_macro", "rh_residual", "ri_residual")
  opt <- list()
  for (id in optimizer_ids) {
    m <- fits[[id]]; dat <- fit_data[[id]]
    alt <- rd_fit(paste0(id, "_bfgs"), formula(m), formula(m, component = "disp"), dat,
      if (startsWith(id, "h") || startsWith(id, "rh")) "height" else "increment",
      stage = "optimizer", family = family(m), second_optimizer = TRUE)
    opt[[id]] <- data.frame(model_id = id, alternative_id = paste0(id, "_bfgs"),
      primary_usable = rd_usable(m), alternative_usable = rd_usable(alt),
      absolute_objective_difference = abs(m$fit$objective - alt$fit$objective),
      max_conditional_prediction_difference = max(abs(predict(m, type = "response", re.form = NA) -
        predict(alt, type = "response", re.form = NA))))
  }
  p2_write(bind_rows(opt), "optimizer-checks")
  loo <- list()
  for (base_id in c("h_diagonal", "i_full", "i_LIDE_macro", "i_SESE_macro")) {
    endpoint <- if (startsWith(base_id, "h")) "height" else "increment"
    m <- fits[[base_id]]; dat <- fit_data[[base_id]]
    for (site in levels(wide$site)) {
      dd <- droplevels(filter(dat, .data$site != .env$site))
      id <- paste0(base_id, "_omit_", match(site, levels(wide$site)))
      alt <- rd_fit(id, formula(m), formula(m, component = "disp"), dd, endpoint, stage = "leave_site_out", family = family(m))
      if (rd_usable(alt)) {
        z <- rd_means(alt, dd, endpoint, id)
        loo[[id]] <- mutate(rd_contrasts(z, endpoint), omitted_site = site)
      }
    }
  }
  p2_write(bind_rows(loo), "leave-one-site-out-contrasts")
}
knitr::kable(p2_read("optimizer-checks"), digits = 6)
```

</details>

The second check leaves out each site in turn. This asks whether one site is
responsible for a treatment difference, and whether the model can still be
fitted with three sites. It does not tell us to remove an inconvenient site.
The existing height checks use `h_diagonal`, while growth checks compare
`i_full`, `i_SESE_macro`, and `i_LIDE_macro`. We are displaying
those saved checks, not fitting additional models.

The plot focuses on the redwood differences we intend to discuss: GS minus HD
and HA minus HD in height, and those same treatment differences in slowing.
A point crossing to the other side of zero means the estimated direction
changes. Missing `i_SESE_macro` points indicate failed fits, not a zero difference.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-site-omission-plot
#| out-width: "100%"
site_review <- p2_read("leave-one-site-out-contrasts") |>
  filter(spp == "SESE", !grepl("later minus earlier", contrast)) |>
  mutate(model = sub("_omit_[0-9]+$", "", model_id),
    omitted_site = factor(omitted_site, levels = c("Whiskey Springs", "Waldo South", "Waldo North", "Camp Six")),
    comparison = factor(contrast,
      levels = c("GS minus HD height", "HA minus HD height", "GS minus HD period change", "HA minus HD period change"),
      labels = c("GS height minus HD height (m)", "HA height minus HD height (m)",
        "GS change minus HD change (m/year)", "HA change minus HD change (m/year)")))
site_plot <- ggplot(site_review, aes(estimate, omitted_site, colour = model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60", linetype = 2) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lcl, xmax = ucl), orientation = "y", width = .15,
    position = position_dodge(width = .35)) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = .35), size = 2.4) +
  facet_wrap(~comparison, scales = "free_x", ncol = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(h_diagonal = "#22665D", i_full = "#777777", i_SESE_macro = "#C56B29")) +
  scale_y_discrete(drop = FALSE) + theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "Estimated difference and approximate 95% interval", y = "Site left out", colour = "Model",
    caption = "Only usable fits are shown. i_SESE_macro failed without Camp Six or Waldo South.")
ggsave(file.path(p2, "figures/site-omission-review.png"), site_plot, width = 10, height = 6.5, dpi = 170, bg = "white")
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(p2, "figures/site-omission-review.png"))
```

**Results and decision.** In `h_diagonal`, the redwood GS–HD height difference stays
positive whichever site is left out, ranging from 3.76 to 5.59 m. HA minus HD
ranges much more widely relative to its size, from 0.05 to 1.58 m. This supports
putting more emphasis on GS versus HD than on the arrangement comparison.
In `i_full`, the estimated GS–HD difference in slowing changes direction across
site omissions, reinforcing our caution about treatment-specific slowing.

The extra terms in `i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro` bring a real fitting concern: both `i_SESE_macro` and
`i_LIDE_macro` fail their numerical checks when Camp Six is omitted, and
`i_SESE_macro` also fails when Waldo South is omitted. Across all the tested
models, 13 of the 16 site-omission fits are usable. **Keep `i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro` as the growth
leading pair, but investigate these failures before accepting their intervals.**
The full four-site `i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro` fits agree under both algorithms; that does not guarantee
stable variation estimates from only three or four sites.

The folded table preserves the exact values behind the plot. It adds detail
for checking a particular model and omitted site, not a different conclusion.

<details>
<summary>Show the redwood site-omission differences and intervals</summary>

```{r}
#| label: rd03-site-omission-review
knitr::kable(p2_read("leave-one-site-out-contrasts") |>
  filter(spp == "SESE", !grepl("later minus earlier", contrast)) |>
  select(model_id, omitted_site, contrast, estimate, lcl, ucl), digits = 3)
```

</details>

### Do the models reproduce the kind of variation we observed?

We compare the observations with 500 datasets already simulated from each
tested model, starting with seed 20261106. This asks whether a model that fits
the averages also produces a believable amount and pattern of variation.
It is different from the later bootstrap, which repeatedly refits models to
check uncertainty in the reported means and differences.

There are three screening tests. The **shape test** (`uniformity_p`) asks
whether observations sit throughout their simulated ranges as expected. For
example, a model that predicts heights too low would leave many observations
near the upper ends of those ranges. The **spread test** (`dispersion_p`)
asks whether the observed variation is too large or too small for the model.
The **extreme-record test** (`outliers_p`) asks whether unusually extreme records
occur more often than expected. These are clues for model review, not a set of
certificates that a model is correct.

In the first three plot panels, a p-value to the left of the dashed 0.05 line is a
reason to look more closely. The fourth panel shows how often the simulations
produce zero or negative responses. A nonpositive *height* is impossible;
a negative change in height can be valid in principle, but none occurs in
this recorded cohort.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-diagnostics
if (recompute) {
  diagnostic_ids <- c("h_diagonal", "h_identity", "h_gamma", "i_full", "i_LIDE_macro", "i_SESE_macro", "rh_residual", "ri_residual")
  diagnostic <- grouped <- macro <- paired <- plots <- list()
  for (k in seq_along(diagnostic_ids)) {
    id <- diagnostic_ids[k]; m <- fits[[id]]; mf <- model.frame(m)
    stopifnot(rd_usable(m))
    set.seed(20261106L + k - 1L)
    sims <- simulate(m, nsim = 500L)
    dh <- createDHARMa(simulatedResponse = as.matrix(sims), observedResponse = model.response(mf),
      fittedPredictedResponse = rowMeans(as.matrix(sims)), integerResponse = FALSE, seed = 20261106L + k - 1L)
    diagnostic[[id]] <- data.frame(model_id = id, simulations = 500L, seed = 20261106L + k - 1L,
      uniformity_p = testUniformity(dh, plot = FALSE)$p.value,
      dispersion_p = testDispersion(dh, plot = FALSE)$p.value,
      outliers_p = testOutliers(dh, plot = FALSE, type = "bootstrap")$p.value,
      simulated_nonpositive_fraction = mean(as.matrix(sims) <= 0),
      observed_nonpositive_fraction = mean(model.response(mf) <= 0))
    rr <- fit_data[[id]] |> mutate(model_id = id, fitted = as.numeric(predict(m, type = "response")),
      residual = as.numeric(residuals(m, type = "pearson")), scaled_residual = dh$scaledResiduals)
    if (!"spp" %in% names(rr)) rr$spp <- "SESE"
    if (!"period" %in% names(rr)) rr$period <- "year10"
    grouped[[id]] <- rr |> group_by(model_id, spp, treat, period) |>
      summarise(n = n(), mean_residual = mean(residual), sd_residual = sd(residual),
        q025 = quantile(residual, .025), q975 = quantile(residual, .975),
        mean_scaled_residual = mean(scaled_residual), .groups = "drop")
    macro[[id]] <- rr |> group_by(model_id, site, plot, spp, period) |>
      summarise(n = n(), mean_residual = mean(residual), .groups = "drop")
    if ("ht_inc" %in% names(rr)) {
      pairs <- rr |> select(model_id, tree, spp, treat, period, residual) |>
        pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = residual, names_prefix = "p")
      paired[[id]] <- pairs |> group_by(model_id, spp, treat) |>
        summarise(n_clumps = n(), conditional_residual_correlation = cor(p5, p10), .groups = "drop")
    }
    plots[[id]] <- rr |> select(model_id, fitted, residual, scaled_residual)
  }
  p2_write(bind_rows(diagnostic), "simulation-diagnostics")
  p2_write(bind_rows(grouped), "grouped-residuals")
  p2_write(bind_rows(macro), "macro-residuals")
  p2_write(bind_rows(paired), "paired-residuals")
  diag_plot <- ggplot(bind_rows(plots), aes(fitted, residual)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey55") + geom_point(alpha = .35, size = .7) +
    facet_wrap(~model_id, scales = "free", ncol = 2) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    labs(x = "Conditional fitted response (m or m/year)", y = "Conditional Pearson residual",
      title = "RD03 exploratory model diagnostics")
  ggsave(file.path(p2, "figures/residual-review.png"), diag_plot, width = 9, height = 9, dpi = 160, bg = "white")
  p2_write(bind_rows(fit_records), "rd03-fit-register")
  writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()), file.path(p2, "tables/session-info.txt"))
}
```

The plot uses the saved test results, so we can see the flagged model directly
without comparing many decimal p-values in a table. Red points mark the low
shape-test result or impossible simulated heights; negative growth changes
are shown as a caution to review rather than the same kind of impossibility.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-diagnostic-flag-plot
#| out-width: "100%"
diagnostic_review <- p2_read("simulation-diagnostics")
flag_data <- diagnostic_review |>
  select(model_id, uniformity_p, dispersion_p, outliers_p) |>
  pivot_longer(-model_id, names_to = "check", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(check = recode(check, uniformity_p = "Shape test: p-value", dispersion_p = "Spread test: p-value",
    outliers_p = "Extreme-record test: p-value"), flag = ifelse(value < .05, "Review", "No screening flag"))
nonpositive <- diagnostic_review |> transmute(model_id, check = "Zero or negative simulated responses (%)",
  value = 100 * simulated_nonpositive_fraction,
  flag = ifelse(grepl("^(h_|rh_)", model_id) & value > 0, "Review", "No screening flag"))
flag_data <- bind_rows(flag_data, nonpositive) |>
  mutate(check = factor(check, levels = c("Shape test: p-value", "Spread test: p-value",
    "Extreme-record test: p-value", "Zero or negative simulated responses (%)")),
    model_id = factor(model_id, levels = rev(diagnostic_review$model_id)))
threshold <- data.frame(check = factor(levels(flag_data$check)[1:3], levels = levels(flag_data$check)), value = .05)
flag_plot <- ggplot(flag_data, aes(value, model_id, colour = flag)) +
  geom_vline(data = threshold, aes(xintercept = value), linetype = 2, colour = "grey55") +
  geom_point(size = 2.8) + facet_wrap(~check, scales = "free_x", ncol = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Review = "#B84B32", `No screening flag` = "#22665D")) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL,
    caption = "Low p-values prompt review; high p-values do not prove adequacy. Growth decreases are possible in principle.")
ggsave(file.path(p2, "figures/diagnostic-flag-review.png"), flag_plot, width = 10, height = 7, dpi = 170, bg = "white")
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(p2, "figures/diagnostic-flag-review.png"))
```

**Results and decision.** `h_gamma` is the only model flagged by the shape test
(p about 0.0015). None is flagged by the overall spread or extreme-record tests.
`h_diagonal` simulates nonpositive heights about 0.47% of the time;
`h_identity` does so about 0.66% of the time. `h_gamma` avoids those heights but
has both a worse AIC and the shape warning. **Do not switch to `h_gamma` just
to remove negative heights. Check the predictions from `h_SESE` and `h_LIDE` before
acceptance instead**, as the later Phase Three review does.

`i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro` simulate nonpositive growth changes about 1.77% of the time for redwood
and 1.25% for tanoak, despite all recorded changes being positive. This is a
limitation to report and inspect, not enough on its own to overturn the large
AIC improvement from `i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro`. The other screening results give no new reason to
change the leading pair, but do not resolve the site-omission failures.

<details>
<summary>Show the eight-model simulation-test results</summary>

The table gives exact p-values, simulation counts, and seed values behind the
plot for anyone checking a particular flag.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-simulation-test-table-review
knitr::kable(p2_read("simulation-diagnostics"), digits = 5)
```

</details>

A residual is the observation minus the model's fitted value, scaled here so
errors from different groups are easier to compare. Positive values mean the
model predicted too low. The existing plot below checks for curves, changing
spread, or unusually large errors that an overall test might hide.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-residual-figure-review
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(p2, "figures/residual-review.png"))
```

The height errors are broadly spread on both sides of zero. Growth errors
have a longer positive side, including some large underpredictions. This is
worth keeping in view when judging the Gaussian growth models, even though
the overall spread and extreme-record tests did not flag them. We do not
interpret a reassuring test as a reason to ignore what the plot shows.

We also check whether many clumps in one macro plot share the same error.
That matters because a cluster of errors in one treatment unit is not many
independent pieces of treatment evidence. The next plot compares `i_full`
with `i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro` using the saved average errors from
each macro plot and period.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-macro-error-plot
#| out-width: "100%"
macro_review <- p2_read("macro-residuals") |>
  filter(model_id %in% c("i_full", "i_SESE_macro", "i_LIDE_macro")) |>
  mutate(plot = factor(plot, levels = sort(unique(as.numeric(plot)))),
    period = factor(period, levels = c("5", "10"), labels = c("Years 1–5", "Years 5–10")),
    panel = factor(paste(model_id, ifelse(spp == "SESE", "(redwood)", "(tanoak)")),
      levels = c("i_full (redwood)", "i_full (tanoak)", "i_SESE_macro (redwood)", "i_LIDE_macro (tanoak)")))
macro_plot <- ggplot(macro_review, aes(plot, mean_residual, colour = period)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey55") +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = .35), size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 2) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("#22665D", "#C56B29")) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "Macro plot (audit ID)", y = "Average error (scaled)", colour = NULL,
    caption = "Positive errors mean predictions were too low. Each point summarizes clumps in one macro plot and period.")
ggsave(file.path(p2, "figures/macro-error-review.png"), macro_plot, width = 10, height = 6.5, dpi = 170, bg = "white")
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(p2, "figures/macro-error-review.png"))
```

`i_full` has average macro-plot errors from about -0.54 to +0.58. In `i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro` they are
closer to zero: about -0.26 to +0.23 for redwood and -0.18 to +0.23 for tanoak.
That is consistent with the usefulness of allowing each macro plot to change
between periods. Some reduction is expected because we fitted those extra
terms, so this is a useful check on *what they do*, not independent proof that
`i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro` are correct. The site-omission instability remains their main numerical concern.

The remaining detailed tables check where errors occur. They do not add a new
main-model recommendation, so they are folded below rather than interrupting
the diagnostic findings.
